title: Amos: let justice roll on like a river

lines: Around 760 BC, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah went north to Israel, which was then at its greatest wealth in generations.
The shrines were crowded, and the rich had houses decorated with ivory. Amos looked beneath the prosperity.

scripture.text: But the LORD took me from following the flock

lines: The book has three parts. A ring of judgments on the nations, which closes on Judah and then on Israel. Sermons, laments, and woes. And five visions, ending in a promise of restoration.

scripture.text: The LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem

lines: It opens with a trap. God judges Israel's neighbors for cruelty every people knows is wrong, and a first hearer would have agreed with every word.
Then the trap closes on Judah, and at greatest length on Israel, who sell the needy for a pair of sandals.

scripture.text: they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.

chapters.kicker: Watch for: justice like a river
lines: God refuses Israel's feasts and songs in some of the hardest words in the Bible.
But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
Amos doesn't reject worship as such. He attacks worship cut off from obedience, and comfort that doesn't grieve.

scripture.text: But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.

lines: In the visions, Amos pleads twice and God relents. Then a plumb line shows Israel out of true.
Amaziah, the priest of the king's shrine, tells him to go home. Amos answers that the LORD took him from following the flock.

scripture.text: I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel

chapters.kicker: Watch for: the fallen tent restored
lines: The book ends in hope. God will restore the fallen tent of David and plant his people in their land.
James quoted these words in Jerusalem, about the Gentiles coming to faith. They make no claim about any modern state or border.

scripture.text: In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David.

lines: Readers across the political spectrum have claimed Amos. The book itself speaks to God's people and their leaders, and its standard is God's covenant, not any modern program or party.
Start with chapter five. Then the key chapters: one, two, three, seven, and nine.
Read the charges for what they name, and let them land on yourself before anyone else.
And hear the invitation inside the warning.
titleCard: Let it land on yourself first.
